messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Threat
  - Threat → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol Fuentes, a sixty-six-year-old divorced Guatemalan American woman, works as a senior editor at a mid-sized publishing house in Chicago. She came to the clinic six weeks ago, describing a presentation that had quietly dismantled her sense of safety over the course of more than a year. Her PCL-5 score of 39 placed her in the clinically significant range, and what emerged across the first several sessions was a portrait of a woman whose internal alarm system had never fully stood down after what she witnessed during a brief but harrowing visit to a conflict-affected region of Central America eighteen months prior.

Marisol had traveled to Guatemala to settle her late mother's estate, a trip she expected to last two weeks. On her third day in the capital, she found herself caught in the street during a military crackdown on a protest near the market district. She heard the explosion before she understood what was happening — a percussion grenade, she was later told, but in the moment it was simply a sound that seemed to remove the floor from beneath her. Soldiers in full tactical gear pushed through the crowd. Among them, she recognized a man she had known decades earlier, a figure connected to state violence during the civil war years, someone her family had feared. He did not appear to see her. She pressed herself against a wall and did not move for a very long time.

In the months that followed her return to Chicago, Marisol found that the world had reorganized itself around that afternoon. Loud, sudden sounds — a car backfiring in the parking garage beneath her office building, a door slamming in the hallway — sent her system into immediate high alert, her heart accelerating, her breath shortening, her body certain that the explosion had returned. Seeing uniformed figures, whether transit police in the subway or security guards in the lobby of her building, produced the same visceral jolt. Each of these triggers, once activated, flooded her with the conviction that she was not safe — that danger was present, proximate, and unresolved. She had come to believe, in a way that no reassurance could touch, that her sense of threat in those moments was accurate rather than historical.

That belief had taken root most deeply in the nights. Marisol described lying awake in her apartment, unable to accept that the darkness outside her windows was simply darkness. She found herself rising two or three times each night to check the locks, to look out onto the street, to confirm that no uniformed figure stood below. She was certain, in the way one is certain of something felt rather than reasoned, that the night hours carried a particular danger — that what had happened in Guatemala was more likely to reach her when she could not see clearly. This sustained nighttime vigilance, exhausting as it was, felt to her like the only rational response to a world that had proven itself capable of sudden violence. And the vigilance itself kept the threat alive: lying awake, scanning, checking, she remained in a state of readiness that made sleep impossible and made the next day's triggers land harder, her nervous system already primed and depleted. The loop tightened week by week. Because she could not feel safe at night, she arrived at her desk each morning already alert, already listening — and so when a sound reached her in the open-plan office, or when a courier in a dark uniform stepped off the elevator, the response was immediate and overwhelming, which in turn confirmed that her nighttime fears had been justified all along.

Over time, Marisol began routing her commute to avoid the transit police checkpoint near her usual station. She stopped attending an evening editorial meeting she had once valued, unwilling to be out after dark. A junior colleague had noticed her distraction and asked whether she was well; Marisol had said she was tired. She had not told anyone what she saw in Guatemala, or who she had seen.

What finally brought her to seek help was a moment at work when a fire drill — the alarm, the sudden noise, the security staff in high-visibility vests moving through the floor — left her unable to return to her desk for the remainder of the afternoon. She sat in a café around the corner and understood, for the first time, that she could not manage this alone. What she most hopes for, she said quietly in their second session, is simply to sleep through the night. What she most fears is that she no longer knows how.
